title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: what would you make a world out of? the Purusha Sukta's answer is an offering, with the seasons as its ingredients

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's proportion: all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven. Did you meet a little more of someone? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

What would you make a world out of? Clay is one answer, shaped by a potter's hands. A spoken word is another. A seed, a shell, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way. The Purusha Sukta gives an answer of its own, and it comes from the fire ritual the hymn itself describes, where offerings are poured into a flame. In this hymn, the world comes from an offering. And the ingredients aren't butter and wood. They're spring, summer and autumn. Today: the great offering.
screen: `CLAY? A WORD? A SEED?` → `THE HYMN'S ANSWER: AN OFFERING.` → `THE INGREDIENTS ARE SEASONS.`

segments.voice: The word is yajna, a sacrifice, an offering poured into fire in Vedic worship. Verse six says that when the gods performed a yajna with the Purusha as the offering, spring was its melted butter, summer its fuel, autumn the offering itself. Hold that picture. A fire ritual where the seasons are what's poured in. The year itself, burning as an offering. Verse seven: on the sacred grass they sprinkled him, the one born in the beginning, and the gods and the seers offered with him. Then come the results. From that offering, fully given, the hymn says, came the creatures of the air, the forest and the village. And verse nine says something that turns the hymn back on itself. From that offering were born the verses and the chants, the meters, the sacrificial formulas. In other words, the Vedas themselves, the very kind of text the hymn belongs to, come out of this first giving. A hymn telling where hymns come from. Verse ten adds horses, cattle, goats and sheep. Readers take this offering in different ways. Some traditional readers treat it as a sacred pattern for the fire rituals that followed: what the gods did first, priests repeat. Others read it more inwardly, as a picture of the one becoming the many by giving itself away. Either way, the shape is clear. In this telling, the world isn't built from the outside, like a house. It comes from something given, and what comes from it, the songs and the animals and the seasons, carries the mark of that giving.
screen: `YAJNA: AN OFFERING INTO FIRE.` · `SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN: THE INGREDIENTS.` · `FROM IT: CREATURES, CHANTS AND VERSES.` · `A WORLD THAT COMES FROM GIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer the season you're in. Settle, and breathe. Notice what season it is where you are: the light, the air, the temperature on your skin. Bring to mind one thing this season has given you lately. A cool morning, a long evening, fruit, rain. Then, on each out-breath, let it go, the way something is poured into a fire. Not lost. Given. If you pray, you can make the out-breath an offering. If not, just let each breath out be a small giving. The bell holds the time.
The Purusha Sukta. In its middle verses, the gods offer the Purusha, with spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it come creatures, chants and verses. Today's word.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. Today, when you give something, time, food, attention, notice what grows out of the giving. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Hindu households and temples keep the practice of offering into fire, and the Purusha Sukta is among the Vedic hymns recited in worship, where its picture of the first offering is remembered.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.6 (when the gods performed the offering with the Purusha, spring was its butter, summer its fuel, autumn its oblation)
Rig Veda 10.90.7–8 (they sprinkled him on the sacred grass; from the offering came the creatures of air, forest and village)

notes: Paraphrase of 10.90.6–10 from memory; confirm order. 6: vasanto asyāsīd ājyaṃ grīṣma idhmaḥ śarad dhaviḥ. 7: on the barhis (sacred grass), the gods, sādhyas and ṛṣis offered. 8: from the sacrifice the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) was gathered; animals of air, forest and village. 9: ṛcaḥ, sāmāni, chandāṃsi, yajus. 10: horses, those with two rows of teeth, cows, goats and sheep.
The hook's 'clay, a spoken word, a seed, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way' lists creation images without naming or comparing any tradition. Confirm it reads as neutral.
The hymn does not describe violence in detail; the script keeps to 'offering' and does not dwell on the Purusha as victim. Confirm tone.
'A fire was kept and offerings were poured into it' describes Vedic household practice generally; confirm.
Editor: removed an unsourced historical claim about Vedic households; verse 7 now says 'sprinkled' (praukṣan) to match the cited text; varied a stock line repeated across nearby days.
